answer: A couple with $130,000 of income can deduct at most $10,000 a year of rental losses against wages: the $25,000 allowance shrinks by 50 cents per dollar of income above $100,000 and is gone at $150,000. Those dollar lines have not changed since their first tax year, 1987. Prices rose by a factor of 2.8334 from 1987 to 2025, so the $100,000 starting line is worth 35.3% of its original value; kept at 1987 value it would be $283,300 (full phase-out at $425,000, allowance $70,800). In 1987 the line sat at 3.84 times the median household income ($26,060); in 2025 it is 1.14 times ($87,460), and the full phase-out is 1.72 times. The couple's $130,000 is about $45,900 in 1987 prices, an income that then got the full allowance; with the lines indexed to prices they could deduct up to $70,800.
guess: Rental property is widely sold as a 'tax shelter'; a middle-income couple would guess that a rental's depreciation-driven paper losses offset their wages in full, or that the limit is aimed only at the rich.
changesDecision: For a $130,000 couple the deductible amount is capped at $10,000 a year and disappears entirely with modest raises, because the income lines that once excluded only high earners now sit barely above the median household. A couple whose purchase math counts on yearly tax savings from losses sees that most losses will be carried forward instead.

numbers.definition: Mean of the 12 monthly CPIAUCNS values for 1987, rounded to 0.001.
Mean of the monthly CPIAUCNS values published for 2025 (11 months; October missing), rounded to 0.001.
Number of 2025 monthly CPIAUCNS values averaged.

price factor k = cpi_2025_avg / cpi_1987_avg, where each is the mean of the monthly CPIAUCNS values published for that calendar year (1987: 12 months; 2025: 11 months, October 2025 was never published), rounded to 0.0001.
100000 * k, rounded to the nearest $100: the 1987 phase-out start expressed in 2025 prices.
150000 * k, rounded to the nearest $100: the 1987 full phase-out point in 2025 prices.
25000 * k, rounded to the nearest $100: the 1987 allowance in 2025 prices.
100 / k, rounded to 0.1: real value of the unchanged $100,000 line in 2025 as a share of its 1987 value.
MEHOINUSA646N value for 1987 (median household income, current dollars).
100000 * median_2025 / median_1987, rounded to the nearest $100: where the line would be if it had grown with median household income.
130000 / k, rounded to the nearest $100: the couple's $130,000 expressed in 1987 prices.
max(0, 25000 - 0.5 * max(0, 130000 - 100000)) = rental loss deductible against other income for a couple with $130,000 of modified adjusted gross income under current law.

Same formula with the $25,000 cap and the $100,000 start both multiplied by k: max(0, 25000k - 0.5*max(0, 130000 - 100000k)), rounded to the nearest $100 (equals the full inflation-adjusted cap because 130000 < 100000k).

assumptions: Married couple filing jointly, actively participating in one rental, modified adjusted gross income $130,000 (wages after pre-tax 401(k) deferrals; the allowance's income measure ignores IRA deductions and some other items).
Not a real estate professional; no short-term-rental exception; losses above the allowance are suspended and carried forward, released when the property is sold.
Prices measured by the CPI-U annual average; 2025 average uses the 11 published months.
Median household income in current dollars, all households (not only married couples, whose median is higher).
limits: Measures the rule against prices and incomes; it does not estimate any rental's actual tax loss, cash flow or appreciation. Median household income series has methodology breaks (e.g. 2013, 2017). Not personal advice.
